article.title: The Unhinged Racist Response to France’s School Protests
article.author: Marlon Ettinger
article.content: After protests and riots swept France this weekend following the escalating social movement sparked by high schooler blockades, right-wingers internationally responded with a straightforwardly racist narrative. They’re portraying the protests as the work of Muslim invaders, in a treasonous alliance with astroturfed left-wingers, who are working to torch the country. “France is burning!” Donald Trump reacted . “The immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country. Close your Borders and take control, before it is too late!” “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn’t listen,” Trump’s vice president, JD Vance, posted in reaction to a video of the bell tower of the Limoges Town Hall falling in flames. “I pray that France, a beautiful country of amazing people, will stop this madness before more of its landmarks burn. And I hope Americans are paying attention. This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country.” The narrative ignores any of the popular demands, including France’s out-of-control cost of living, a degraded school system, and legitimate explosive anger over the murderous violence the police unleashed on high schoolers at the beginning of the month. Since the movement began, replacing such concerns with blind-to-reality, downright racist grievance-mongering has been the official line taken by international reaction. “What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration,” Trump posted to an official White House government account early this month, as the movement started making global headlines. “This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!” “Europe opened its borders and failed to confront radical Islamism,” Texas Senator Ted Cruz commented then. “AOC, Mamdani, El-Sayed, and Talarico want to take us in this direction.” “We need to recognize that the pro-Palestinian protests are fundamentally protests against the West, and their ambitions are much greater than eradicating Israel from the river to the sea,” hedge fund billionaire Bill Ackman bloviated in response to a chairwoman of a Berlin-based think tank describing a video of protesters chanting “We’re all children of Gaza” as the beginning of an “Islamic Revolution in Europe.” “In Iran, it took roughly two years to go from this stage to complete chaos and the establishment of the Islamic Republic,” that chairwoman, Maral Salmassi, who helms the Zera Institute, wrote . “We saw the same symbolism, the same flags, and heard the exact same slogans. Brace yourselves.” Fox News echoed and boosted the theme early on, publishing an investigation on October 9 attempting to delegitimize the student movement by portraying it as a global conspiracy between communists and Islamists. “A transnational network of 50 groups mobilizes around student protests, only 1/3 are youth groups,” read the breathless subheading of the piece, which claimed to have uncovered a globe-spanning operation of “far-left communist and socialist organizations” who are using the “fiery student protests” to push a “political and ideological agenda.” France’s hysterical racists, boosted by far-right American media organizations devoted to pushing racist propaganda, also weighed in early on. “You have to be blind not to see what’s happening here,” Thaïs d’Escufon, the former spokesperson for the since dissolved French white nationalist group Génération identitaire , told One America News host Chanel Rion, describing the student protests as “ethnic riots.” “They only show footage of the students of the bourgeoisie, of the center of Paris, but actually most of the protests are from cities or areas with a lot of replacement,” d’Escufon explained, using “replaced” to mean areas with a lower percentage of whites. “It’s hard to see this footage. . . . You look at this and it doesn’t look like Paris,” Rion emoted after showing overhead footage of an anonymous crowd of protesters at the Place de la Nation in Paris after a march. “It looks like Mogadishu. . . . And yet you saw the photo that the BBC used. They make it look like it’s just native French students upset by a lack of blackboards.” Fox’s investigation has also endorsed the idea that the media has sanitized the movement by portraying it as “students protesting [against] deteriorating school conditions.” In reality, Fox claimed, the movement “is. . . . part of an extensive infrastructure of unions, communist activists, far-left political parties and international media organizations. . . . [who] are organizing demonstrations, calling strikes, mobilizing supporters and broadcasting the unrest around the world.” Fox’s investigation argues that only fifteen of the fifty organizations involved in the movement are actual student groups, and among those groups are communist youth movements and a Muslim student association. Singling out the communist and Muslim organizations, Fox concludes that there’s a “‘red-green’ alliance of leftists with Muslims.” “The communist Red and the Islamist Greens have nothing in common but a common enemy, the Judeo-Christian, capitalist, free West, led by the U.S.,” Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation, told Fox. “Their goal is to dismantle us.” British fascist Tommy Robinson has attacked the movement on similar grounds. “The ‘French students’ are destroying Paris again right now,” he joked last week, above a video of French police running past a burning car. This past Wednesday, Robinson attacked Bally Bagayoko, the France Insoumise mayor of Saint-Denis, in a post linking to a video of Bagayoko announcing a restriction on selling alcohol around the city’s train station between 7 pm and 6 am. “Bally Bagayoko made history in March 2026 by becoming the first Black and Muslim mayor mayor of Saint-Denis,” Robinson wrote . “Joined the invader riots last week. Today he announced a ban on alcohol. Wake the fuck up France.” Al-Trojan House The messaging echoes a pernicious narrative in French media that has sought to portray any political organizing by French Muslims as a self-evident Trojan horse for Islamism. “Behind demands about the degraded situation of high schools, the Étudiants musulmans de France (EMF) organization and its allies push their battle against ‘state islamophobia,’” reads a subheading from a story in Le Point claiming that “Islamist networks” are trying to amplify the movement. The article points to a Muslim student organization it claims a government report last year identified as the youth branch of the Muslim Brotherhood. Accusing organizations like EMF of “recuperating” the protests, the article says posts from the organization “speak volumes” about their strategy. One offender from the beginning of the month is a statement in support of the high schoolers’ fight “for a decent and dignified learning environment.” EMF’s statement goes on to oppose government austerity in public services, including universities; a law that raises fees for foreign students; government measures canceling rent subsidies for foreign students; “university partnerships with genocidal and ecocidal businesses”; the selective and “racist” system of university admissions; and government repression of the protests. Le Point also points to AJ+, the Qatari-funded social media wing of Al Jazeera , for their viral social media output highlighting atrocious school conditions and police violence as a vector for spreading this narrative. “Most of them return to the topic of police violence, without a word about the protesters’ [violence], and accuse the ‘mainstream media’ of lying about the ‘violence’ of the marches,” the Le Point article reads. A Liberal Response Massive protests over the weekend of at least a half million people descended into violence, with the police in Paris reportedly losing control of the situation as black bloc militants and vandals took advantage of the chaos to loot some of the city’s toniest quarters. Videos like the clip of the Limoges bell tower falling in flames went viral as examples of destruction being wrought by Third World “barbarians” on Eternal France. “I hope the world is paying attention to the riots in France,” said Tim Kennedy , a celebrity soldier and MMA fighter. “There are no French flags being flown at these protests. This is the consequence of mass immigration.” The idea that there were no French flags being flown at the protests is a flat-out lie. I saw many over multiple days . But the post is representative of the hardening of the narrative laid down earlier in the month. Pro-European liberals also joined in on the hand-wringing and condemnation. “Poland will not repeat the mistakes of other European countries, nor will it pay for them,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced without making a direct reference to the protests in France. “We are firmly defending the border against illegal migration, we have our own asylum policy (we do not accept applications), we deport those who break Polish law.” “Shocking videos and images are coming out of France,” Hungarian President Péter Magyar posted. “In the face of this senseless destruction and unjustified violence, perhaps it is now clear to everyone why Hungary advocates the strictest possible approach to migration, and why we will not weaken our border protection or immigration policy under any pressure.” Feckless American liberals, while condemning the straightforwardly racist framing and acknowledging that the student protesters are “an extremely diverse coalition,” have flirted with the narrative. Thomas Chatterton Williams, in a piece in The Atlantic titled “The Violence Sweeping France Was Never Really About Schools,” dismisses any real content in the protests after a review of five viral social media clips. “Much of the protesting by students has become an exercise in nihilistic resentment. . . . beneath the pretext of school reform,” Williams writes, pointing to clips showing acts of violence, property damage, or students rallying and shouting, often from social media aggregator accounts that push an anti-immigrant narrative, frequently portraying Arab and African immigration in Europe as a Trojan horse for Islamism. “The violence hasn’t been limited to one side,” Williams admits charitably, drawing parallels between students making anti-police declarations in crowds or singing along to rap songs with distasteful references to terrorism and life-changing, disfiguring injuries inflicted on students by the police. “A police officer fired a tear gas grenade at a teenager’s head, knocking out most of his teeth. More recently, a 15-year-old lost his hand after an officer fired a stun grenade.” At the end of the day France is “at the mercy of protesters,” Williams argues. “The French protest too much,” and “in recent years, France’s protest culture has been indulged and glorified to the point of insanity.” “Some of these demands may be valid,” Williams allows, “but the violence fanning out across France has little to do with pedagogical concerns.” Protesting Right French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu made a similar argument on Thursday when he claimed that the social movement was “no longer a high schoolers’ movement” but a “movement of urban violence, the intensity of which has increased further in recent days.” In a speech on Sunday evening, President Emmanuel Macron blamed the violence from the night before on “troublemakers from far-left splinter groups, joined by numerous delinquents,” while Lecornu denounced the supposedly “important role” of France Insoumise presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his party in fomenting it. While the French government hasn’t engaged in the same grotesquely racist theories of the American, British, and French far right, they are united with them in their narrative that this social movement is the product of outside, illegitimate forces that are trying to instrumentalize the demands of the high schoolers. That point was driven home particularly forcefully in a report from the Le Canard enchaîné on Wednesday, which revealed that Lecornu had personally directed the interior minister to explore the idea of prosecuting Mélenchon for “inciting rebellion.” Lecornu only backed off after getting cold feet about what type of effect jailing Mélenchon might have on the movement. The paper reported nearly seven thousand arrestees over the past three weeks, 86 percent of whom were between the ages of fourteen and eighteen. Authorities made around two thousand additional arrests over the weekend. “The goal of the tactic is to frighten the students and their parents into stopping the uprising as quickly as possible,” one chief of police told Le Canard . The government remains scared of this social movement because of the fact that it isn’t a foreign plot, the work of immigrant invaders, or an ” Islamo-leftist ” conspiracy. Powerful racists will continue to push the idea that it is because it’s a convenient way to wipe away the demands of the masses, but it won’t change the reality on the ground. Macron’s government has brought violence to France’s streets. A report on Monday morning that Macron rejected the Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez’s offer to resign sends a clear message that he supports what the police are doing despite last night’s pro forma calls for dialogue and rote condemnation of violence. French students have legitimate demands, and many of them are determined to continue protesting until the government answers them. This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture.
